statement: In the late evening hours of May 16, 2025, a large and deadly nocturnal EF4 tornado moved through the Kentucky cities of Somerset and London.
The tornado was on the ground for almost an hour and a half.
The tornado killed 19 people.
The tornado injured 108 others along a 60 mi (97 km) track.
The tornado produced damage that was rated EF4 by the National Weather Service in Jackson, Kentucky.
This violent tornado occurred as part of a major tornado outbreak that spanned from May 15 to 16.
The supercell that produced this tornado initiated over 400 miles (640 km) away in the south-central Missouri Ozarks region.
The supercell produced few tornadoes along its track through Missouri, Illinois, and Kentucky.
The supercell produced a small but intense EF3 tornado that brought destructive impacts to the area south of the village of Blodgett.
Several homes suffered major damage due to the EF3 tornado near Blodgett.
Mobile homes were destroyed due to the EF3 tornado near Blodgett.
Trees were snapped due to the EF3 tornado near Blodgett.
Two fatalities occurred due to the EF3 tornado near Blodgett.
Ten others were injured due to the EF3 tornado near Blodgett.
Afterwards, the supercell crossed the Ohio River into Kentucky.
The supercell produced a brief EF1 tornado near Lamasco.
The supercell produced an EF2 tornado near Allegre, damaging or destroying several mobile homes and outbuildings.
After the London tornado dissipated, the supercell eventually got absorbed into the mesoscale convective system.
The tornado first touched down in central Russell County.
The tornado initially caused minor damage to trees and infrastructure.
The tornado quickly intensified to EF3 strength.
The tornado inflicted major damage to a home near Whittle.
The tornado weakened and shrunk after crossing into Pulaski County.
After crossing Lake Cumberland, the tornado struck the southern side of Somerset at low-end EF3 intensity.
The tornado inflicted severe to major damage to several homes and businesses in Somerset.
After leaving the city, the tornado tore through parts of the Daniel Boone National Forest at mid-range EF3 to low-end EF4 intensity.
The tornado shredded and snapped several trees as it entered Laurel County.
The tornado destroyed a couple of homes as it entered Laurel County.
The tornado then impacted the southern side of London at low-end EF4 intensity.
The tornado inflicted catastrophic destruction to several homes and neighborhoods in London.
The tornado resulted in several fatalities in London.
The tornado dissipated shortly after near the community of Lida.
The tornado was on the ground for 90 minutes.
The tornado tracked for 60 miles (97 km).
Recovery efforts immediately following the tornado were intensive.
Several aid organizations, including The Salvation Army and the Federal Emergency Management Agency, traveled to London with relief supplies.
Following the tornado, media outlets claimed the National Weather Service office in Jackson, Kentucky was understaffed due to staffing cuts made by the Department of Government Efficiency.
The National Weather Service office in Jackson, Kentucky was fully staffed at the same time of the tornado.
On May 12, the Storm Prediction Center outlined a Day 5 risk for the middle Mississippi River valley.
A pacific front associated with May 15 convection was expected to stall across the middle Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys before moving north as a potent warm front.
Ensemble Guidance models at the time were hinting at dewpoints reaching between mid to upper 60s, possibly reaching into low 70s.
Ensemble Guidance models at the time were hinting at the likelihood of one or more linear segments to traverse across the mid-Mississippi, lower Ohio, to potentially into Tennessee valleys.
On May 14 at 0730 UTC, The Storm Prediction Center outlined a slight (2/5) risk over much of the Ozark Plateau, Mississippi and Ohio River Valleys.
The slight risk included the possibility of seeing scattered discrete supercells, organized clusters, and the chance of a long-lived mesoscale convective system.
Medium and long-range guidance models suggested the development of thunderstorms along the warm front.
A surface trough ahead of the mid-level wave was suggested to mature by medium and long-range guidance models.
The models depicted an environment where the mean level convective available potential energy (MLCAPE) values were around 3000 J/kg.
The models depicted an environment where effective bulk shear was 40-50kn.
The depicted environment had thermodynamic/kinematic conditions supporting the development of long-lived severe weather.
There were still uncertainties around the event.
Persistent disagreement among models was evident in regards to the northward extent of the warm sector.
Some recent model runs showed the likelihood of persistent morning convection.
Other model runs showed less morning convection.
In the evening hours on the same day at 1730 UTC, an enhanced (3/5) risk was outlined for most of the lower Ohio Valley.
The enhanced risk included one or more organized cluster and a couple more discrete supercells.
An upper-level trough over the southern High Plains was expected to traverse quickly across the Midwest.
Strong mid to upper southwesterly flow was expected to overspread the region.
The 500 mb jet stream was forecasted to be around 70-90kn.
A highly moist airmass was forecasted to be in place extending from southern Missouri into southern Illinois and into northeast Ohio.
Increased southerly flow ahead of the cold-front allows the warm-front along the I-70 corridor to lift north throughout the afternoon.
Strong destabilization was forecasted to occur as a result of steep mid-level from cooling aloft and dewpoints of mid to upper 60s.
Low-level jet around 45-60kn was forecasted to overspread the region due to peak daylight heating into the evening.
The Storm Prediction Center outlined a moderate (4/5) risk over much of the middle Mississippi and lower Ohio Valleys on May 16.
The greatest risk was over southeastern Missouri, far northeastern Arkansas, northwestern Tennessee, southern Illinois and Indiana, far southwestern Ohio, and much of Kentucky.
The upper-level low centered over the border of North Dakota and Minnesota was expected to move eastward into the middle Mississippi Valley.
Following persisting convection from the previous day, a warm front swept over a large region from Missouri to the Ohio and Tennessee Valley regions.
Over this region, the atmosphere was expected to sharply destabilize.
Mean level convective available potential energy (MLCAPE) values were expected to exceed 2500 J/kg over this region.
Strong mid-level flow was expected over this region.
Deep-layer wind shear exceeding 50 kn (58 mph; 93 km/h) was expected to help develop and intensify severe weather and associated supercells over this region.
The 06z outlook issued by Chris Broyles and Harry Weinman mentioned the risk of 'a high-end long-track tornado...from far southeast Missouri...into western Kentucky'.
The tornado first touched down in Russell County northeast of Jamestown at 10:26 p.m. EDT.
At the touchdown point, the tornado damaged the roof of an outbuilding.
The tornado started eastward and crossed KY 619.
The tornado shattered windows and inflicted roof and siding damage to a home before crossing Caney Creek.
The tornado uprooted trees on the hillsides on both sides of Caney Creek.
The tornado then turned east-northeastward, rolling and destroying a mobile home before crossing McFarland Creek.
The tornado moved into Whittle and crossed KY 1611.
The tornado partially removed the roof off a home and an outbuilding as it moved east-northeastward and crossed KY 76.
The tornado rapidly intensified to high-end EF2 intensity after crossing KY 76.
The tornado significantly debarked and stubbed hardwood trees.
The tornado destroyed mobile homes and a camper.
The tornado then crossed Alligator Creek and continued east-northeastward at low-end EF2 strength.
The tornado snapped and uprooted trees.
The tornado destroyed a garage.
It then briefly strengthened to low-end EF3 intensity as it crossed Gosser Ridge Road.
The tornado unroofed and destroyed most of the exterior walls of a one-story brick home.
Another home sustained major EF1 roof damage.
Several trees nearby were snapped.
The small tornado maintained low-end EF3 intensity as it crossed into Pulaski County.
The tornado continued eastward across House Fork Creek and Wolf Creek, stubbing and debarking hardwood trees.
The tornado then weakened slightly and struck a farmstead on a Cundiff Road at high-end EF2 strength.
The tornado unroofed a home and destroyed several outbuildings as well as a small and large solo at the farmstead.
The tornado then briefly reached low-end EF3 intensity on Cooks Chapel Road.
The tornado unroofed and knocked down the exterior walls of a home and stubbed more trees on Cooks Chapel Road.
It then weakened significantly to low-end EF2 intensity as it crossed KY 196.
The tornado unroofed another home, heavily damaged or destroyed multiple outbuildings, and snapped trees as it crossed KY 196.
The tornado then narrowed and weakened further to EF1 intensity as it continued eastward and passed south of Faubush.
The tornado damaged outbuildings and snapped trees along KY 1664.
One small area of EF2 damage occurred on Oakes Road.
A property on Oakes Road suffered considerable roof and exterior damage.
The tornado then continued eastward at EF1 intensity as it passed south of Nancy and crossed KY 761 and KY 235 while gradually shrinking in size.
Homes suffered roof damage.
Outbuildings were destroyed.
More trees were snapped.
The tornado then crossed Clifty Creek and struck a neighborhood south of KY 80.
The tornado caused heavy EF1-EF2 roof damage to homes and snapped trees and power poles in the neighborhood south of KY 80.
The tornado then narrowed even further and crossed Fishing Creek at EF1 strength before descending a steep hillside across KY 1577.
After crossing KY 914 and entering the southern side of Somerset, the tornado strengthened and reached EF2 intensity as it continued down the hillside.
Two homes were destroyed in Somerset.
Other homes and an apartment building suffered heavy roof and exterior wall damage in Somerset.
Vehicles were damaged in Somerset.
Trees were snapped or uprooted in Somerset.
The tornado then impacted the Somerset Cinemas 8 building.
About 100 people were inside Somerset Cinemas 8 watching movies at the time the building was struck.
The Somerset Cinemas 8 building received minor roof and structural damage.
A strip mall along Parkers Mill Way received major damage to its roof at mid-range EF2 strength.
The southside wall of the Pulaski County Area Technology Center sustained complete collapse.
Along US 27/KY 1642, the tornado intensified to high-end EF2 intensity.
The Redeemer Lutheran Church of Somerset received heavy damage.
The front and back walls of the Redeemer Lutheran Church of Somerset collapsed.
Major roof damage was noted to occur at the Redeemer Lutheran Church of Somerset.
Multiple trees and power poles around the church were snapped or twisted.
Adjacent to the church, the Baxter's Coffee restaurant also sustained major damage.
The roof of Baxter's Coffee restaurant was torn away.
Two walls of Baxter's Coffee restaurant collapsed.
The Speedway and South Central Bank received significant roof and structural damage.
Metal and electric power poles around the Speedway and South Central Bank were snapped.
The Hardee's restaurant had all their windows blown out.
The sign at Hardee's restaurant was broken and bent.
Afterwards, the tornado sustained high-end EF2 intensity as it crossed Southern School Road.
The Independent Opportunities Community Hab was completely flattened.
Other nearby metal buildings sustained significant damage.
Along Regency Drive and Weddle Lane, the tornado intensified to low-end EF3 strength.
The tornado removed most of the roof and second story of the recently built Warrior Martial Arts building.
At the South Kentucky Rural Electric Cooperative Corporation facility, the tornado inflicted major damage to the main office building.
The tornado unroofed and collapsed most of the warehouse next to the South Kentucky Rural Electric Cooperative Corporation main office building.
From there, the tornado continued eastward at EF2 intensity.
The tornado damaged a metal building system.
The tornado destroyed a small shed.
The tornado snapped more trees and power poles.
More trees were snapped or uprooted at a farm.
A small barn was shifted off its foundation at the farm.
A silo was destroyed at the farm.
Metal roofing was removed from a building at the farm.
Several vehicles were damaged at the farm.
Around a dozen homes and 20 businesses were destroyed in the Somerset area.
The tornado then crossed KY 914 again, snapping and uprooting swaths of trees as it exited Somerset.
After crossing Pitman Creek, the tornado demolished an outbuilding along Doc Newell Road before crossing the Cincinnati Southern Railway.
The tornado impacted a home along KY 2747 at low-end EF3 intensity.
A poorly built home was blown off its foundation.
The tornado maintained low-end EF3 intensity after crossing KY 1247.
The tornado impacted a small neighborhood along Curtis Ray Road.
Several homes were substantially damaged in the neighborhood along Curtis Ray Road.
The homes closest to the tornado's path were partially leveled.
Several trees were snapped or uprooted.
An outbuilding was destroyed.
Cars and trailers at a junk yard were moved or flipped over.
Along Elihu Cabin Hollow Road, a recently built barndominium/metal framed house was completely swept away at mid-range EF2 intensity.
Most of the debris from the barndominium/metal framed house was unable to be located.
A shed on this property was thrown 100 yd (91 m) clockwise to the other side of the home.
Downstream from the home, another group of homes were impacted at high-end EF2 intensity.
A top part of a home was torn away, leaving the subfloor left.
A small outbuilding nearby was destroyed.
Multiple trees were downed and uprooted around the property.
Southwest of the community of Alcalde, the tornado intensified to low-end EF3 strength.
Along KY 769, a large transmission tower was crumpled and thrown 250 yd (230 m).
Several softwood trees were severely debarked.
A home was unroofed and its side exterior walls collapsed.
Two barns were wiped clean off their foundation.
Several trees were substantially snapped and uprooted.
The tornado continued to produce heavy EF2 tree damage as it moved eastward.
It knocked over an RV and collapsed a metal barn on KY 1643.
The tornado then moved into the Daniel Boone National Forest and quickly intensified to EF3 strength.
The tornado splintered and debarked swaths of trees as it grew in size.
North of the community of Poplarville along KY 3269, the tornado intensified to low-end EF4 intensity for the first time.
A one-story concrete foundation home was leveled.
Three people were taking shelter in the leveled home: an elderly couple and a friend.
Two people survived from the leveled home.
The wife, a 69-year-old woman, was killed by flying debris and was later found in the yard of the home.
Several nearby outbuildings on the property were obliterated and swept away.
A car was heavily damaged.
Several trees behind the property were extensively debarked and stubbed.
The tornado then weakened as it continued eastward and crossed KY 192 at EF2 intensity.
Another area of intense tree damage occurred east of KY 192.
The tornado regained EF3 intensity east of KY 192.
This included extreme tree damage with only stubs and heavily debarked softwood trees left behind.
Surveyors assessed the wind speeds to be at 153 mph (246 km/h).
153 mph (246 km/h) is the highest wind speed rating for damage to softwood trees.
Surveyors noted that the tornado was likely at EF4 intensity here.
After briefly weakening to EF2 intensity, the tornado regained EF3 intensity as it approached KY 1003 while continuing to grow in size.
Entire swaths of softwood trees were mowed down, debarked, and stubbed as the tornado approached KY 1003.
Surveyors noted that the tornado may have reached EF4 intensity multiple times along this segment of the path.
The tornado reached its maximum width of just under a mile as it crossed KY 1003.
Several homes were heavily damaged or destroyed as the tornado crossed KY 1003.
Some homes had some or all of their exterior walls knocked down as the tornado crossed KY 1003.
Two mobile homes and outbuildings were blown away as the tornado crossed KY 1003.
Vehicles were damaged as the tornado crossed KY 1003.
Power poles were damaged as the tornado crossed KY 1003.
The tornado then crossed into Laurel County, continuing to mow down swaths of trees.
After crossing the county line, the tornado began to shrink in size and weaken slowly as it continued eastward.
The tornado dropped to EF2 intensity along W Line Creek Road.
The tornado then began impacting large residential areas southwest of London.
The tornado first impacted the Laurel Canyon subdivision at high-end EF2 intensity.
Multiple homes had their roofs completely removed and exterior walls knocked down in the Laurel Canyon subdivision.
Other homes suffered minor to moderate roof damage in the Laurel Canyon subdivision.
Wooden power poles were snapped in the Laurel Canyon subdivision.
Several trees and power poles were snapped or uprooted in the Laurel Canyon subdivision.
The tornado then shrank some more and weakened further to EF1 intensity.
The tornado damaged or destroyed outbuildings and snapped or uprooted trees.
It then exited the forest and crossed KY 192 again, removing most of the roof off a home.
The tornado strengthened to high-end EF2 intensity along Hart Church Road.
Extensive tree damage occurred along Hart Church Road, with several trees snapped.
Multiple homes experienced significant roof damage along Hart Church Road.
One home along Hart Church Road had most of its walls leveled.
A 47-year-old woman was killed along Hart Church Road when her home suffered major damage.
The tornado then briefly lifted above the tree line as it descended another hill before touching back down at the bottom of the hill.
The tornado intensified further to high-end EF3 intensity as it impacted the Lovelace Subdivision and Wyan Road.
Three homes were swept away in the Lovelace Subdivision.
An unanchored, elevated two-story vinyl home was thrown across Wyan Road.
Several other homes received significant damage in the Lovelace Subdivision.
Some homes in the Lovelace Subdivision were leveled or had only interior walls left standing.
Other homes nearby had severe roof damage.
Outbuildings were destroyed in the Lovelace Subdivision.
Vehicles were damaged in the Lovelace Subdivision, including a tractor-trailer that was turned to its side.
Trees and power poles were snapped in the Lovelace Subdivision.
An elderly couple was killed in one of the homes in the Lovelace Subdivision.
The tornado maintained high-end EF3 intensity, impacting the south and southeastern parts of the Sunshine Hills subdivision.
Three homes were completely leveled or swept away in the Sunshine Hills subdivision.
One of the leveled homes had a concrete slab that was lifted and cracked, as the small room on the slab was ripped away.
Poor construction quality prevented a higher rating for the leveled home.
Several mobile homes were obliterated in the Sunshine Hills subdivision.
Many outbuildings were swept away in the Sunshine Hills subdivision.
The tornado then became violent once again with winds of 170 mph (270 km/h).
The Sunshine Hills Baptist Church was completely swept off its foundation, leaving sections of the basement intact.
Two well-built brick homes beside the church were mostly destroyed, leaving a few interior walls standing.
To the east of the church, across the street, another row of homes was destroyed.
Trees in this area were violently debarked and denuded.
One of the trees had twisted metal wrapped around it.
The tornado crossed over Walker Lane, demolishing a row of three homes at low-end EF4 intensity.
The tornado crossed Boone Trail, leveling and sweeping away several more homes off their foundations.
A 68-year-old elderly woman was killed in her home along Boone Trail.
The tornado continued onto Sunshine Hills Road, sweeping away one home and heavily damaging others.
A concrete porch from the swept home was shifted 10–20 ft (3.0–6.1 m) and was cracked in half.
The family in the swept home survived with minor injuries.
Two homes were mostly leveled, leaving a few interior walls standing.
A man was killed in one of the mostly leveled homes.
Another one-story brick home was completely flattened.
Several softwood and hardwood trees were heavily debarked and stubbed.
The tornado weakened slightly to high-end EF3 intensity, impacting the Saddlebrook Garden Homes.
A couple of poorly constructed homes were leveled and swept away at estimated windspeeds up to 160 mph (260 km/h).
Several other homes were mostly leveled, with a few interior walls standing.
Many softwood trees were extensively debarked.
A 67-year-old retired woman was killed in one of the homes along Saddle Road.
Most of the casualties from this tornado occurred in the Sunshine Hills subdivision.
At least nine fatalities occurred in the Sunshine Hills subdivision alone.
The tornado then crossed KY 363 and I-75 and weakened to mid-range EF3 intensity as it impacted a neighborhood and mobile home park along Philpot Road.
A poorly built home was swept away along Philpot Road.
Several mobile homes were destroyed along Philpot Road.
Multiple homes sustained moderate to significant roof damage along Philpot Road.
Two one-story houses had their exterior walls collapse along Philpot Road.
A garage was destroyed along Philpot Road.
Several trees were snapped along Philpot Road.
The tornado weakened further to mid-range EF2 intensity, impacting another neighborhood along Hawkins Road and McGill Pine Grove Road.
Multiple homes sustained significant roof damage along Hawkins Road and McGill Pine Grove Road.
Several broken glass windows were observed along Hawkins Road and McGill Pine Grove Road.
Trees were snapped or uprooted along Hawkins Road and McGill Pine Grove Road.
The tornado continued northeast and impacted another subdivision along KY 1006.
Another poorly built home along Airview Drive was impacted.
Another home along Airview Drive was mostly leveled, with a few interior walls left standing.
Multiple outbuildings and garages were destroyed in this subdivision.
A couple of homes sustained minor to severe roof damage in this subdivision.
A mobile home was obliterated in this subdivision.
Trees were severely debarked and denuded in this subdivision.
Another poorly built home was leveled at mid-range EF3 intensity in this subdivision.
Two elderly siblings were killed in this subdivision as their home was destroyed here.
The tornado continued eastward, crossing over the runway of the London-Corbin Airport before impacting the Meadowlane Subdivision near the airport.
Initially impacting at low-end EF3 intensity, two mobile homes along Court Road were demolished.
A home had large sections of its roof ripped away along Court Road.
Several other homes sustained moderate roof damage along Court Road.
The tornado intensified slightly along Oak Road.
A couple of homes were destroyed along Oak Road, with interior walls left standing.
A couple more homes along Oak Road had their exterior walls collapse.
An unanchored home was shifted off its foundation along Oak Road.
Several homes along Meadowlane Road had extensive roof damage, and some of their walls collapsed.
The tornado intensified further along Meadowlane Road.
Two homes were mostly leveled along Meadowlane Road, with interior walls left standing at estimated windspeeds up to 150 mph (240 km/h).
Around the same time, a security camera from across the runway captured the tornado tearing through the subdivision at 11:47 p.m. EDT.
The tornado crossed Miller Lane, leveling another poorly constructed home at the same intensity.
A detached garage was leveled on the property along Miller Lane.
The tornado slightly intensified to estimated winds of 155 mph (249 km/h) along Miller Lane cul-de-sac.
Three rows of homes were leveled along Miller Lane cul-de-sac.
The poor construction quality negated a higher rating for the leveled homes along Miller Lane cul-de-sac.
A few other homes were left with their interior walls intact along Miller Lane cul-de-sac.
Trees were severely debarked along Miller Lane cul-de-sac.
Another home with subpar construction was leveled along Miller Lane cul-de-sac.
The tornado maintained EF3 intensity, impacting several warehouses and hangars south of the main airport building.
Several hangers and metal building systems were significantly damaged.
A couple of hangers and metal building systems were destroyed.
A couple of aircraft, including six Beechcraft T-34 Mentors and a medical helicopter, were thrown and destroyed.
The tornado reached high-end EF3 intensity, impacting a large metal building along Airport Drive.
The entire structure of the large metal building was completely destroyed, with debris swept clean from the foundation.
The I-beams of the large metal building were torn loose from their anchoring.
The Soelberg Industries manufacturing center was leveled by the tornado.
The Maximus Industrial building along KY 1006 was heavily damaged by the tornado.
The tornado inflicted severe damage to the exterior walls and parts of the interior walls of the Maximus Industrial building.
A family of three was taking shelter inside the Maximus Industrial building.
Their 25-year-old son was killed by the tornado as the Maximus Industrial building collapsed.
Near the Maximus Industrial building, a small neighborhood was impacted.
Two one-story brick homes in the neighborhood had parts of their exterior walls collapsed.
Several homes in the neighborhood were unroofed.
A mobile home in the neighborhood was badly damaged.
A large tree in the neighborhood was uprooted.
The tornado then crossed US 25, strengthening slightly to low-end EF3 intensity as it impacted a small business sector along the highway.
The Triple Threat Martial Arts school and a large apartment building along US 25 were completely destroyed.
Two fatalities occurred inside the apartment building along US 25.
The Southside Florist shop was flattened, with estimated windspeeds up to 140 mph (230 km/h).
Adventure Pets pet store was heavily damaged.
None of the pets inside Adventure Pets were killed.
Three exotic birds worth thousands of dollars were missing from Adventure Pets and considered stolen.
The C & R Auto Repair shop was flattened.
A strip mall suffered heavy exterior walls damage.
Afterwards, the tornado crossed the CSX CC Subdivision and impacted a two-story home along Levi Jackson Mill Road, inflicting major damage to the structure.
A small cabin nearby was unroofed.
Several trees were snapped or uprooted along Levi Jackson Mill Road.
An outbuilding was destroyed along Levi Jackson Mill Road.
The Loughran's Olympic Boxing & Martial Arts building was significantly damaged, with parts of the structure being ripped away.
The tornado then went through the forested areas of the Levi Jackson Wilderness Road Park, crossing KY 229 and impacting the Laurel County Fairgrounds.
The tornado destroyed a couple of warehouses at the Laurel County Fairgrounds.
The tornado snapped trees and power poles at the Laurel County Fairgrounds.
The tornado uprooted trees at the Laurel County Fairgrounds.
The Slate Hill Baptist Church was unroofed at EF2 intensity.
The tornado intensified slightly to high-end EF2 strength for the final time, impacting the Crooked Creek Golf Club neighborhood.
A home along the intersection of Crooked Creek Road and Cedar Ridge Drive was heavily damaged.
Another home along Cedar Ridge Drive was also heavily damaged, leaving a few interior walls standing with estimated windspeed up to 135 mph (217 km/h).
Two other homes sustained significant roof damage in the Crooked Creek Golf Club neighborhood.
After impacting the first couple of homes along Cedar Ridge, the tornado abruptly weakened significantly.
The tornado mainly shattered windows, snapped or uprooted trees, and caused light roof damage at EF1 strength.
After exiting the neighborhood, the tornado continued eastward, causing EF0-EF1 damage to trees before weakening further to EF0 strength after crossing Farris Road.
From there, the tornado crossed KY 521, KY 830, KY 80, and KY 488, mainly causing minor tree damage.
A home along KY 830 also suffered minor damage.
The tornado then dissipated west of Lida just after crossing KY 488 at 11:56 pm EDT.
The tornado was on the ground for 90 minutes.
The tornado tracked 60.08 mi (96.69 km).
The tornado reached a peak width of 1,700 yd (1,600 m).
Laurel County declared a mass casualty incident.
In all, 19 people were killed.
Seventeen of the killed people were in London.
One person was killed in rural Pulaski County.
One woman was killed in Russell County.
At least 108 others were injured as reported from the CHI St. Joseph Hospital in London.
The tornado was preliminary rated EF3 before being upgraded to EF4 several days later.
Nineteen people were reported as killed as a direct result of the tornado.
Of the nineteen killed, seventeen of the deaths occurred in London.
Other deaths occurred in rural Pulaski and Russell counties.
The first recorded death in Russell County since the 1974 Super Outbreak was due to this tornado.
The tornado was the deadliest in Eastern Kentucky on record.
At least one of the deaths occurred in the Sunshine Hills subdivision, where a family with an unspecified number of members was killed.
A grove of trees saved the lives of a family in the Sunshine Hills subdivision.

Survey teams noted that 'the only thing that likely saved this house and its occupants was the grove of trees located behind it, on the southwest side, which took the brunt of most of the debris coming from the houses upstream, while also delimbing and debarking the trees in the process'.
A couple, a major firefighter from the Laurel County Fire Department and his wife, were thrown 150–300 ft (46–91 m) into a field after the tornado destroyed their home.
The firefighter was killed.
His wife was left in critical condition.
One person in a home on the subdivision had to receive an amputation as a result of damage from the tornado.
The tornado was rated EF4 at this person's property.
Another couple each lost an arm as they were sheltering next to each other during the tornado.
A family that was sheltering in their home was thrown as their residence was swept away, but the family survived with minor injuries.
News agency Fox Weather wrote that the subdivision itself looked 'unrecognizable'.
The New York Times said that the tornado was 'out of a horror movie'.

Local authorities in Somerset feared that the death toll would've been high in the city if the tornado had veered into more populated subdivisions along Parker Mills Road or had touched down during daylight, where the business district would have been very active with employees and customers.
In the wake of the tornado, the Saint Joseph Health Hospital in London saw an influx of patients.
More than 100 people were treated in the Saint Joseph Health Hospital.
One person died at the Saint Joseph Health Hospital.
The majority of patients at Saint Joseph Health Hospital were treated and released.
Eleven patients were sent to other hospitals from Saint Joseph Health Hospital.
Four patients were admitted to Saint Joseph Health Hospital.
In total, 108 patients were treated for injuries, ranging from cuts to punctured lungs and bruises.
The age range of the patients treated were from one-year-old to elderly individuals.
At least ten others were injured by the tornado.
Eight people remained in hospitals according to a WLEX-TV publication on May 17.
The tornado damaged or destroyed 1,500 homes.
The tornado caused $350 million (2025 USD) in damage in Laurel County alone.
The tornado received a rating of EF4 on the Enhanced Fujita scale following a damage survey.
The tornado was classified as violent based on the damage it caused.

Meteorologist Chuck Grier at the NWS office in Jackson said that 'to get one of those in our area is quite rare and quite an impressive coming together of atmospheric conditions', referring to the tornado.
According to the damage survey, EF4 damage was inflicted between two different areas along the tornado's 59.9 mi (96.4 km) track.
The first portion of EF4 damage occurred in the Daniel Boone National Forest east of Somerset.
A farmhouse was completely destroyed in the Daniel Boone National Forest.
Trees were debarked and denuded in the Daniel Boone National Forest.
The United States Forest Service advised visitors to avoid areas in advance of windfall.
The second portion of EF4 damage occurred within London city limits.
Seventeen homes in the Sunshine Hills subdivision west of the London-Corbin Airport sustained EF4-rated damage.
Almost consistent EF3-rated damage was inflicted by the tornado as it moved through the Daniel Boone National Forest.
Thousands of trees were leveled by the tornado.
The tornado traveled 47 miles (76 km) through the forest.
The tornado swept through almost 30,000 acres of trees in the forest.
The highest rating that softwood trees in the forest could receive was mid-range EF3.
Damage surveyors noted that there was 'complete timber devastation' in the forest.
Damage surveyors noted that the wind speeds were likely higher than mid-range EF3 in the forest, including at an area near Mount Victory.
Initial state assessment estimated that more than $59 million is needed to clean up more than 1.5 million cubic yards of debris from buildings and vegetation in Somerset and London.
Mayor of Somerset, Alan Keck, reported that 20 businesses in the commercial area and dozens of homes were damaged or destroyed by the tornado.
Aerial video taken by several drone operators and storm chasers in the days following the tornado showed extreme damage in London.
Aerial footage was shared widely by news agencies.
Damage from the tornado was also visible on satellite imagery.
As of 2025, it is one of three tornadoes to inflict EF4 rated damage within the state of Kentucky.
It is the second-deadliest EF4 tornado in Kentucky post-2007 after the 2021 Western Kentucky tornado.
The tornado was the strongest ever surveyed in National Weather Service Jackson's 'county warning area'.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) was dispatched to London to help with immediate recovery efforts.
Kentucky governor Andy Beshear praised the federal response to the tornado, stating 'but they've done a good job when FEMA has come in to Kentucky, and I'm grateful'.

Senator Rand Paul remarked on FEMA's operations immediately following the tornado, saying 'talking with the emergency management people here, they feel like the federal government—and same in Pulaski County—the federal government is doing a pretty good job right now'.
Operation Barbecue Relief were mobilized in London to serve meals to survivors and first responders.
Operation Barbecue Relief expected to serve 1,500 meals per day in Kentucky.
The Team Kentucky Storm Relief Fund, established by Governor Andy Beshear, and United Way of Laurel County Long-Term Disaster Fund accepted any donations for the places impacted by the tornado.
The Salvation Army volunteers offered meals and emotional and spiritual care in Somerset on May 17 and in London the next day.
The Salvation Army volunteers served lunch and dinner at the Creek Church in Somerset for victims and volunteers on May 19.
At the Creek Church, the tornado provided 200 to 300 hot meals per day to victims impacted by the tornado.
Looting occurred after the tornado.
Looters stole donations at the Bill Vaughn Memorial Trailer Park in London.
More donations poured in after the looting.
Samaritan's Purse sent out two disaster relief units tractor trailers filled with supplies and equipment.
Unit seven of Samaritan's Purse set up a base of operation at the Calvary Baptist Church in London.
Perry County Fiscal Court officials organized multiple drop-off locations to collect supplies to help victims of the tornado in London.
Residents of Perry County were urged to donate items, which included tarps for temporary shelter, protection and gift cards for food, and other essential supplies.
Kroger donated $25,000 (2025 USD) to God's Pantry Food Bank for the communities impacted by the tornado.
Kroger stores in Laurel and Pulaski counties donated 24 packs of water to the areas impacted by the tornado.
Kroger donated a box truck of hygiene products and shelf-stable food to the Laurel County Sheriff's Office to a shelter that was set up at the Laurel County High School.
Walmart and its foundation and Sam's Club partnered with nonprofit organizations to provide resources to London.
Walmart and its foundation and Sam's Club raised $750,000 to support relief efforts.
The Walmart Superstore located in London offered free meals through the support of Operation BBQ relief.
Meade Tractor donated $100,000 (2025 USD) to the city of London to aid in recovery efforts.
Other organizations participated in relief and recovery efforts immediately following the tornado.
On May 30, a town hall meeting was held in London for people affected by the tornado to ask questions about the event and discuss disaster relief in the town.
FEMA and the American Red Cross were in attendance at the town hall meeting.

The same day, Governor Beshear stated that more funding was needed for recovery efforts, saying 'what I'm seeing are expenses that are large enough to where I think a SAFE fund will be needed, especially for Laurel and Pulaski counties'.
FEMA declared six Kentucky counties a disaster area on May 23 under the identification number 'DR-4875-KY', after a request for aid assistance was submitted by Beshear.
The six counties declared a disaster area included Russell, Pulaski and Laurel counties.
Beshear estimated that cleanup costs would likely total over $59 million (2025 USD).
Beshear estimated that 1,500,000 yards (4,500,000 ft) of debris will need to be removed from areas where the tornado impacted.
The issuance of tornado warnings during the event, and staffing cuts as a whole at the National Weather Service in Jackson, Kentucky, were a talking point following the tornado.
Due to staffing cuts caused by the Department of Government Efficiency, the three major NWS offices in Kentucky were all understaffed at the time of the tornado outbreak.
Despite the cuts, the Jackson office was prepared to be fully staffed on May 16 due to the upcoming severe weather event.
Christian Cassell, one of the lead meteorologists at the office, stated that 'we saw the risk many days ago. We were already planning how we would staff days in advance'.
Fact-checking website Snopes refuted the claim that tornado warnings were not issued for Somerset and London as a result of staffing cuts.
United States President Donald Trump allegedly initially delayed sending disaster relief to areas hit by the tornado, leaving people pleading the government for aid.
On May 24 governor Beshear's request for government-led aid was approved.
The approved aid included grants for temporary housing and loans to cover uninsured property losses.
A video taken of the tornado in Pulaski County was posted on social media.
Television station WYMT-TV displayed the video live.
In Somerset, a security camera located on a Pro Fab, Inc. building captured the tornado's winds shortly before the building was destroyed.
At 11:47 pm EDT, the tornado was captured on the London-Corbin Airport's south-facing security camera.
Shortly after the tornado entered the camera's viewing range, it cut power to the airport.
The tornado was captured on camera as it passed over the Levi Jackson Park area south of London.
